concepts.name: The Three Crowned Kings (Muvendar): Political Structure and Rivalry
key_dimensions: Distinction between Cheras, Cholas, and Pandyas — capitals, emblems, and core territories
Nature of their polity: tribal chieftaincy vs. nascent monarchy — degree of state formation
Inter-Muvendar conflicts and the role of battle poetry (Purananuru) as historical evidence
UPSC trap: Confusing Sangam-age Cheras/Cholas/Pandyas with their medieval successors of the same names

concepts.name: Concept of 'Vel' Chiefs and the Hierarchy of Chieftains (Ventar, Vel, Kilar)
key_dimensions: Three-tier political hierarchy: Ventar (kings) > Vel (chiefs) > Kilar (village headmen)
Economic basis of chieftaincy: cattle raids, tribute, and gift redistribution (kадai system)
Role of chiefs as patrons of poets and its political significance
UPSC trap: Distinguishing this decentralised chieftaincy model from the centralised Mauryan bureaucracy

concepts.name: Sangam Assemblies (Sangams): Historicity and Literary Tradition
key_dimensions: Legend of three Sangams at Madurai — mythological vs. historical interpretation
Only the Third Sangam considered historically credible and its surviving corpus
Role of Pandyan kings as patrons of the Sangam academies
UPSC trap: Treating all three Sangams as equally historical; the first two are largely legendary

concepts.name: Tinai System: Ecological Zones and their Socio-Political Significance
key_dimensions: Five Tinais: Kurinji (hills), Mullai (forests/pastoralism), Marudam (agriculture), Neytal (coastal), Palai (arid) — and their associated themes
Each Tinai linked to a specific deity, flower, bird, and emotional mood (akam poetry)
Tinai as a tool for understanding Sangam economy, ecology, and social organisation
UPSC trap: Confusing Palai as a separate geographical zone vs. it being a transformed/arid version of other zones

concepts.name: Akam and Puram Poetry: Nature, Themes, and Historical Value
key_dimensions: Akam (interior/love poetry) vs. Puram (exterior/war, death, heroism poetry) — structural distinction
Akam poetry as indirect historical evidence for social norms, gender roles, and caste relations
Puram poetry (e.g., Purananuru, Patirruppattu) as direct evidence for political history and warfare
UPSC trap: Akam poetry is NOT a direct historical source; its value is sociological and inferential

concepts.name: Sangam Economy: Trade, Craft, and the Role of Roman Commerce
key_dimensions: Key ports: Puhar (Kaveripattinam), Muziri (Muchiri), Korkai — their commodities and hinterlands
Evidence from Periplus of the Erythraean Sea and Ptolemy's Geography for Indo-Roman trade
Nature of exports (pepper, pearls, muslin) and imports (wine, gold, horses)
UPSC trap: Roman gold coin finds in South India are evidence of trade, NOT of Roman political control

concepts.name: Social Stratification in Sangam Society: Caste, Varna, and Tribal Identity
key_dimensions: Sangam society was NOT rigidly caste-based in the Brahmanical Varna sense — tribes and occupational groups coexisted
Emergence of Brahmin influence and Aryanisation of Tamil society during the later Sangam period
Presence of Paraiyas and Pulaiyas — evidence for early forms of untouchability or occupational segregation
UPSC trap: Projecting later medieval caste rigidity onto the more fluid Sangam social structure

concepts.name: Position of Women in Sangam Society
key_dimensions: Evidence from Akam poetry for relatively greater agency — love, choice of partner, expression of grief
Institution of 'Sati' (Karpu/Pativrata ideal) and widow immolation — evidence and debate
Women poets (Avvaiyar, Nappinnai) and their social status as exceptions vs. norm
UPSC trap: Akam poetry reflects idealized literary conventions, not necessarily real social conditions for all women

concepts.name: Concept of 'Nadу' (Nadu): Local Self-Governance Unit
key_dimensions: Nadu as a territorial unit below the kingdom — its administrative and fiscal functions
Role of Ur (village assembly) and Nadu in revenue collection and local dispute resolution
Continuity of the Nadu system into the Pallava and Chola periods — long-term institutional significance
UPSC trap: Do not confuse Nadu (territorial unit) with the concept of Nadu in Tinai classification

concepts.name: Eight Anthologies (Ettuttokai) and Ten Idylls (Pattupattu): Content and Significance
key_dimensions: Ettuttokai: Akananuru, Purananuru, Ainkurunuru, Kuruntokai, Kalittokai, Narrinai, Patirruppattu, Paripatal
Pattupattu as longer poems — Silappatikaram and Manimekalai are NOT part of Pattupattu (common confusion)
These texts as primary sources for Sangam polity, trade, and social life
UPSC trap: Placing Silappatikaram within Sangam anthologies — it is a post-Sangam epic, not part of Ettuttokai or Pattupattu

concepts.name: Silappatikaram and Manimekalai: Epics as Historical Sources
key_dimensions: Silappatikaram (Ilango Adigal) — themes of justice, urban life, port trade, and the three kingdoms
Manimekalai (Sattanar) — Buddhist philosophical epic; evidence for Buddhism in Tamil Nadu
Both epics as sources for urban centres (Puhar, Madurai, Vanji) and social conditions
UPSC trap: These are post-Sangam (3rd–6th century CE) works, not classical Sangam-period compositions

concepts.name: Tirukkural (Thiruvalluvar): Nature, Content, and Dating Controversy
key_dimensions: Three books: Aram (virtue/dharma), Porul (polity/wealth), Inbam (love) — secular and ethical content
Dating debate: 1st century BCE to 5th century CE — implications for its Sangam vs. post-Sangam classification
Absence of sectarian religious identity — neither exclusively Jain, Buddhist, nor Brahmanical
UPSC trap: Tirukkural is often placed in Sangam literature for convenience, but its dating and authorship are contested

concepts.name: Role of Brahmins and Vedic Religion in Sangam Tamil Society
key_dimensions: Brahmin presence in Sangam texts as advisors, poets (e.g., Kapilar) and ritual specialists
Tension and synthesis between Dravidian religious practices (Murugan worship) and Vedic Brahmanical traditions
Evidence of Aryanisation: Vedic sacrifices (yagnas) performed by Tamil kings to legitimise authority
UPSC trap: The Sangam age was NOT uniformly Brahmanical — Buddhism, Jainism, and folk traditions were equally significant

concepts.name: Buddhism and Jainism in the Sangam Age: Evidence and Influence
key_dimensions: Jain influence: Tirukkural's possible Jain authorship debate; Jain monasteries in Tamil Nadu
Buddhist influence: Manimekalai as Buddhist text; Buddhist viharas at Kaveripattinam
These traditions as counter-forces to Brahmanical orthodoxy before the Bhakti movement
UPSC trap: The decline of Buddhism and Jainism in Tamil Nadu came AFTER the Sangam age, driven by the Bhakti movement (post-6th century CE)

concepts.name: Concept of 'Kадai' (Gift-Giving) and the Patron-Poet Economy
key_dimensions: Poets as a professional class dependent on royal/chiefly patronage — economic implications
Gift economy as a political tool: chiefs gained legitimacy and fame through generosity (vallan)
Panegyric poetry (praising kings) as ideological state apparatus in a pre-bureaucratic polity
UPSC trap: The patron-poet relationship was NOT purely literary — it was a key mechanism of political legitimation

concepts.name: Warfare and the Concept of 'Vetchi' (Cattle Raid) in Sangam Polity
key_dimensions: Seven types of war situations (Tinai of Puram) — Vetchi (cattle raid) as the most common trigger
Economic basis of war: cattle as primary wealth in pastoral-agrarian economy
Institution of 'Maravars' (warrior caste) and the culture of heroic death (Virali/Nadukkal memorial stones)
UPSC trap: Sangam warfare was largely small-scale, cattle-raid based — NOT organised conquest wars like Mauryan campaigns

concepts.name: Hero Stones (Nadukal/Virgal): Evidence for Social and Military History
key_dimensions: Hero stones as archaeological evidence corroborating Sangam literary sources on warfare
Iconographic analysis: depictions of battle scenes, ascent to heaven, and divine honours
Geographic distribution as evidence for the spread of the warrior culture across South India
UPSC trap: Hero stones are NOT exclusive to the Sangam age — they continue into the medieval period, requiring careful dating

concepts.name: Sangam Age Urbanisation: Puhar (Kaveripattinam) as a Case Study
key_dimensions: Puhar as a cosmopolitan port city — evidence from Silappatikaram and archaeology
Presence of foreign merchants (Yavanas/Greeks), diverse communities, and guild organisations
Urban-rural economic linkages: nadу supplying the port city; port distributing imported goods inland
UPSC trap: Urbanisation in Sangam South India was port-driven and trade-oriented, distinct from the planned Indus Valley cities or Mauryan administrative centres

concepts.name: Yavanas (Greeks/Romans) in Sangam Literature and their Role
key_dimensions: Yavana as a generic term for Western foreigners — Greeks, Romans, and later Arabs all called Yavanas
References in Sangam poetry to Yavana torchbearers, wine, and guards in Tamil courts
Archaeological evidence: Roman amphorae, coins, and pottery at Arikamedu (Pondicherry)
UPSC trap: 'Yavana' in Sangam texts does NOT exclusively mean Greeks — it is a broad term for Western/foreign people

concepts.name: Tolkappiyam: Earliest Tamil Grammar and its Socio-Political Content
key_dimensions: Structure: Three books — Ezhuttatikaaram (phonology), Sollatikaram (grammar), Porulatikaram (poetics/social norms)
Porulatikaram as a source for understanding Tinai, social hierarchy, and gender norms
Dating controversy: claimed to predate Sangam anthologies, but possibly contemporaneous or later
UPSC trap: Tolkappiyam is primarily a GRAMMAR text — its social content is secondary and inferential, not a straightforward historical chronicle
